Black carbon, methane, and ozone; known as super pollutants, drive nearly half of global warming and pose major health risks. Though short-lived, they have a far greater warming impact than CO₂, making their reduction a fast and effective way to slow climate change. Experts at the WHO Air Pollution and Health Conference stressed that cutting these emissions could serve as an “emergency brake” on climate change while preventing millions of deaths from air pollution. Despite their impact, super pollutants remain underregulated, with black carbon notably absent from the Paris Agreement. Addressing these pollutants could rapidly reduce warming, protect food security, and improve public health, offering a crucial opportunity for immediate climate action. Well articulated Sophia Samantaroy!

Sophia Samantaroy

1y

Just three pollutants - black carbon, ozone, and methane - are responsible for nearly half of global temperature increases.

Reducing these emissions, which only remain in the atmosphere for a few weeks to decades, could serve as the “emergency brake” critical to halting runaway #climate change, said experts Monday on the eve of the second World Health Organization Air Pollution and Health Conference.

“If you reduce them today, we’ll see impacts in our lifetimes,” said Claire Henly, executive director of the Super Pollutant Field Catalyst, a US start-up NGO, at a media briefing ahead of the conference.

While CO2 has received the overwhelming amount of climate mitigation attention, Henly and others argued that addressing a class of “super pollutant” greenhouse gases and particles, also known as “short-lived climate pollutants,” offers the greatest opportunity to have a rapid, and meaningful impact on both health and climate.
Henly and others identified ozone, black carbon, and methane as super pollutants because of their wide-ranging impacts on food security, health, and climate change. Slowing the rate of climate change would make it easier for the “world to adapt to climate change,” said Henly.

Types of Carbon You Should Know 💡 💡

When we talk about climate change, we often hear the word carbon—but did you know it exists in different forms, each playing a unique role in our planet’s climate system? Let’s break it down 👇

🖤 Black Carbon
Produced from the incomplete combustion of fossil fuels, biomass, and forest fires. A major component of soot, it absorbs sunlight and worsens global warming while also polluting the air.

💙 Blue Carbon
Carbon stored in coastal ecosystems such as mangroves, seagrasses, and salt marshes. These ecosystems are natural climate heroes, capturing and storing large amounts of CO₂.

🤎 Brown Carbon
Light-absorbing organic carbon from burning biomass (wood, crops, etc.). Unlike black carbon, it can both warm and cool the atmosphere depending on conditions.

❤️ Red Carbon
Carbon released through biological particles on snow and ice—affecting reflectivity and accelerating melting.

💚 Green Carbon
Carbon stored in terrestrial ecosystems—forests, plants, and soils—forming a vital part of the natural carbon cycle.

✨ Understanding these types of carbon helps us see both the threats and the opportunities in the fight against climate change. Protecting ecosystems, reducing emissions, and managing carbon wisely are key to a sustainable future.

“When food is wasted, all the resources that went into producing it are also wasted”
-Tristram stuart, National Geographic Explorer, winner of International Environment Award and Sophie prize (2011) for his fights against food waste

Today marks the International day of Awareness of Food Loss and Waste - a reminder that our daily choices regarding our food system and related system flaws are contributing to a global climate crisis.
Every bit of food wasted carries invisible carbon footprint in terms of energy and water used to produce it. Food lost or wasted end up in landfills, which contribute to about 8-10% of all human generated greenhouse gases as a result of anaerobic decomposition. Landfills are responsible for 11% of total anthropogenic methane emissions, which act as a thick blanket trapping heat and consequently leading to global warming.
By focusing on innovative solutions, ranging from better supply chain management to composting and biomethanation, we can turn this huge climatic crisis into an opportunity for a more sustainable future

🌍 Climate Mitigation: Tackling the Root Causes of Climate Change

When we talk about climate change, two words often stand out: adaptation and mitigation. Adaptation is about coping with the changes already happening, like building flood defenses or adjusting farming practices. But mitigation is about preventing the problem from getting worse by addressing its root causes.

At its core, climate mitigation focuses on reducing greenhouse gas emissions and enhancing activities that absorb carbon from the atmosphere. Without strong mitigation efforts, adaptation alone will not be enough.

🔹 So, what does mitigation look like in action?

Clean Energy Transition: Shifting away from fossil fuels and investing in renewable sources like solar, wind, hydro, and geothermal. This reduces emissions from the energy sector the single largest contributor to global warming.

Energy Efficiency: Designing smarter cities, greener buildings, and efficient industries that use less energy but deliver more.

Sustainable Transport: Expanding public transport, promoting electric mobility, and creating walkable cities that reduce reliance on fossil-fuel vehicles.

Agriculture & Land Use: Moving towards climate-smart agriculture, reducing methane from livestock, and promoting sustainable food systems. Reforestation, afforestation, and protecting wetlands also act as vital carbon sinks.

Innovation & Technology: Exploring solutions such as carbon capture and storage, renewable-powered industries, and circular economy approaches that minimize waste.

Policy & Finance: Governments and institutions adopting carbon pricing, emission trading systems, and green financing models to accelerate the shift toward low-carbon economies.

🌱 Mitigation is not just a technical challenge, it’s also a societal transformation. It requires collective action, behavioral change, and bold leadership. Every individual choice, whether reducing food waste, conserving energy, or supporting greener businesses, contributes to the bigger picture.

The world has committed to limiting global warming to 1.5°C and achieving net-zero emissions by 2050. These are not just political targets; they are life-saving goals. If we succeed, we can avoid the most devastating impacts of climate change, safeguard ecosystems, and build healthier, more resilient communities.

✨ The time for half-measures is over. Climate mitigation is not just about reducing risks; it’s about creating opportunities, for innovation, for green jobs, for cleaner air, and for a sustainable future that benefits us all.

International Climate Action Day — 24 October 🌱

Climate change isn’t just a buzzword — it describes the long‑term shifts in temperature, weather patterns, rainfall, and more. While Earth’s climate does naturally vary, what’s happening now is amplified by human activity, especially the burning of fossil fuels, deforestation, and excessive CO₂ emissions. Energy Wired

Why does it matter? Because rising global temperatures drive extreme weather, disrupt ecosystems, threaten food and water security, and undermine the wellbeing of people all over the world — including right here in Australia. (And yes, we are affected too.)

But we can act. Here’s what you can do to reduce your impact and become part of the solution:

Switch to renewable energy (solar, wind, etc.) so your power comes from clean sources rather than fossil fuels

Reduce energy use at home — turn off lights/appliances, avoid standby mode, upgrade to more efficient devices

Cut back on travel — walk, cycle, use public transport, carpool, or switch to electric vehicles

Reuse, repair, recycle — ask yourself: do I need a new item, or can I repurpose what I have?

Avoid single‑use plastics & support products with lower carbon footprints

Plant trees, support conservation efforts, and advocate for policies that protect our planet

🌍 Air Pollution & Climate Quiz

1. Air Quality Index (AQI) is a number that ranges from 0 to 500. Which number indicates the most polluted air?
➡️ 500

2. Certain chemicals once used in sprays and refrigerators were banned worldwide because they damaged the ozone layer. What are they called?
➡️ Chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs)

3. Which gas is the most produced greenhouse gas from burning coal, oil, and gas, contributing to global warming?
➡️ Carbon dioxide (CO₂)

4. What four-letter word, a combination of smoke and fog, is used to describe many forms of air pollution?
➡️ Smog

5. Which is the main cause of acid rain – air pollution or water pollution?
➡️ Air pollution

6. Chronic exposure to ground-level ozone primarily affects which human body system?
➡️ Respiratory system

7. What is the greenhouse effect?
➡️ The way greenhouse gases trap and hold heat, warming the Earth and atmosphere.

8. What are the three main greenhouse gases?
➡️ Carbon dioxide (CO₂), methane (CH₄), nitrous oxide (N₂O)

9. Forests are called the “lungs of the Earth.” How do they help reduce air pollution?
➡️ Trees take in carbon dioxide and release oxygen, making the air cleaner.

10. Why are electric cars better for air quality?
➡️ They don’t burn fuel or release greenhouse gases, so they reduce air pollution.

🌍 **Fossil Fuels vs. Food: Climate Impact**

When it comes to climate change, fossil fuels are the main culprits. They cause over 75% of global greenhouse gases and almost 90% of CO₂ emissions. In contrast, agriculture contributes about 20–30% of emissions.

🔍 **Key Points**:
- Fossil fuels (coal, oil, gas) are the top source of climate emissions.
- A small group of companies produce most fossil fuel emissions.
- Burning fossil fuels, not our food choices, is the bigger problem.

🔧 **What Can You Do?**:
- Reduce your fossil fuel use. Support policies that promote renewable energy.
- Stay informed to dispel myths about climate impacts and focus discussions on major issues.
- While making eco-friendly food choices is beneficial, prioritize reducing fossil fuels.
- Advocate for holding major emitters accountable for their emissions.

"12. The statutory setting being thus plain, the
municipality cannot extricate itself from its responsibility.
Its plea is not that the facts are wrong but that the law is
not right because the municipal funds being insufficient it
cannot carry out the duties under Section 123 of the Act.
This 'alibi' made us issue notice to the State which is now
represented by counsel, Shri Gambhir, before us. The plea
of the municipality that notwithstanding the public
nuisance financial inability validly exonerates it from
statutory liability has no juridical basis. The Criminal
Procedure Code operates against statutory bodies and
others regardless of the cash in their coffers, even as
human rights under Part III of the Constitution have to be
respected by the State regardless of budgetary provision.
Likewise, Section 123 of the Act has no saving clause when
the municipal council is penniless. Otherwise, a profligate
statutory body or pachydermic governmental agency may
legally defy duties under the law by urging in self-defence
a self-created bankruptcy or perverted expenditure
budget. That cannot be.

12. A perusal of the photographs of the compensatory plantation show the
following:

(a) the sapling planted are only shrubs of small height and will take
years before they become trees of some considerable size;

(b) No comprehensive record of the plantation has been maintained by
the Department of Forests and Wildlife and NCRTC; and

(c) The region of plantation may not be feasible since the same is a
flood prone area. (as per the statement of the learned Amici).

13. To my mind, the condition of the transplanted trees along with the
compensatory plantation clearly indicates a failure on the part of the
Department of Forest and Wildlife and the NCRTC to integrate nature along
with development. There is no doubt that the development of a city is of
primary importance but the trees cannot be left at the mercy of infrastructural
expansion, without any consideration of their survival. Trees are not a
dispensable commodity but it doesn't appears that the transplantation of trees
along with the compensatory plantation have been done with that
understanding.

14. Courts have consistently held that compliance must be meaningful,
effective, and aligned with the spirit of the order, rather than being a
mechanical or a meaningless exercise. When a court issues directions, it does
so with a specific intent. If such intent and objective is not met, then it cannot
be said that the compliance is actually done.

15. This court is bound to ensure that the rights of the citizens to enjoy a
clean and healthy environment under Article 21 of the Constitution of India is
not infringed by the Departments. Without a balance being struck between
development and nature, we risk creating a concrete jungle, devoid of green

felled/transplanted by the NCRTC for the Delhi-Meerut RRTS Corridor

regarded as a dispensable resource and their removal and transplantation must
be carefully evaluated in the context of environmental sustainability, urban
planning, and the necessity of the project.

19. The intention of this court has never been to be an impediment to
growth and development but the endeavour is to ensure that the said
growth/development is not done at the cost of public health and
environmental sustenance.
